chunks: Muhammad ibn Ali Majiluwayh narrated to us. He said: My uncle Muhammad ibn Abi al-Qasim narrated to us, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from al-Mufaddal, from Jabir, from Abu Ja’far al-Baqir (peace be upon him).
Regarding the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ‘And speak beautifully to the people’ [2:83].

He said: Say to the people better than what you would like to be said to you, for indeed Allah, Mighty and Majestic, hates the persistent curser, the habitual insulter, the frequent condemner of the believers, the obscene and the deliberately vulgar, the importunate beggar; and He loves the modest, the forbearing, the virtuous, and the self-restrained.

key_terms.الحيي: al-hayiyy — the modest, one with haya (modesty/shame)
key_terms.المتعفف: al-muta’affif — the self-restrained, one who guards one’s chastity and dignity

ai.seo_question: What does Islam say about speaking kindly to people?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (AS) interprets Quran 2:83 (‘Speak beautifully to the people’) by establishing a golden rule of speech: one should say to others what is better than what one would wish to hear oneself. He then contrasts the traits Allah detests — habitual cursing, insulting believers, obscenity, and importunate begging — with those He loves: modesty, forbearance, virtue, and self-restraint. This teaching was delivered in the context of early Islamic community building, where interpersonal conduct was central to the cohesion of the believers.
